newsitem.title: JAPAN: WEEK AHEAD - Nikkei average to aim for 19,000.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Nikkei average to aim for 19,000.

text.p: The Tokyo stock market's benchmark index is likely to aim for the 19,000 level this week amid continuing support from pension funds, which have been active buyers in recent sessions.

"Bargain-hunting by pension funds as well as foreign investors reshuffling their portfolios should support the Nikkei average in times of weakness," said Ken Ishikida, Sanyo Securities general manager. "But the upside is heavy near the 19,000-line, and the rise will be gradual."
The Tokyo stock market benchmark has climbed about 1,000 points over the last two weeks, boosted mostly by pension funds eager for blue chips.
On Friday, the 225-share Nikkei average closed 85.21 points or 0.46 percent lower at 18,612.86, but was still up about 260 points on the week.

"The pace (of gains) has been rather rapid, with the Nikkei average steadily clearing technical points such as the 18,750.25 intra-day high," said a broker at a medium-size firm. "It could challenge the 19,229.49 intra-day high set on February 24."
Brokers said that with the bulk of the first round of pension fund allocations nearly spent, market participants were wondering who would buy what after the funds run dry.
"It's not clear how foreign investors are going to move and what's going to happen to currencies, so no one can guess who will buy after the pension funds stop," said a source at a foreign brokerage.

Brokers said that unless the yen moved excessively in either direction, stock indices were unlikely to be affected much. Institutional investors had been stocking up on low-priced domestic demand-led issues to hedge against the strengthening of the yen, they added.
"Once the fresh money stops, there may be an over-supply, and the market could be forced to correct itself and wait for fresh allocations," a "Big Four" broker added.
However, some strategists said that with corporate earnings due to be announced in the coming weeks, investors may be inspired and decide to buy shares based on firm earnings prospects.
"Upward revisions stemming from the recent weakness of the yen against the dollar will be welcomed by investors," said Haruo Nakaharu, a Toyo Securities director.
Market sources said more firms may choose to unveil plans for share repurchases and stock options in order to beef up their share prices, making some issues attractive for investors.

"The impact of the two percentage point consumption tax increase on retailers in April should also become clearer and if the effect is smaller than expected, then that too will be encouraging," Nakaharu added.
